title: Grab wafers between which are wedged lumps of coal and copper snow
html_source:
This whole episode is a wild and weird Witches Sabbath, and its phantasmagorical method makes it difficult to maneuver. The initial scene has us guessing at what it is we’re looking at when the narrator describes a cart owned by the “real” Antoni Rabaiotti dispensing ice cream, surrounded by squabbling “stunted” men and women, who greedily “grab wafers between which are wedged lumps of coal and copper snow.” They’re all “children,” the narrator explains. The immediately available choices for interpretation are, of course, many and diverse: Are the figures children who are “stunted” future adults? Are they merely callow adults acting immaturely? A deeper search by the reader will reveal that this first scene hearkens back to the Wandering Rocks episode, where children are eating ice cream by Rabaiotti’s ice cream cart when they encounter a one-legged sailor who “growls” at them. That he is a sailor is why the children order him to salute.

Of course, nothing has to make sense in this surreal setting, but, since Joyce is not one to “waste” his imagery, a carnival atmosphere such as this at the gateway to the carnal, when the root of “carnival” is carne vale, or “farewell to flesh,” with vale representing a Latin “good-bye” (literally “be strong” or “be well”), it is difficult not to see this as yet one more jab at Irish lechery-born paralysis, especially when, after clamoring for the ice cream, and having sucked on what turns out to be lumps of coal and copper snow, the children “scatter slowly” in apparent chagrin.

What we will encounter repeatedly in Circe are glimpses into past passages in the book that now take on completely different understandings – epiphanies. This chapter is about sudden enlightenment – epiphany (among other things).
